analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal regulator dedicated to policing unsafe and predatory consumer financial products.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in March 2009, referred to the House Financial Services Committee, and never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created an independent Financial Product Safety Commission — a government agency whose single job would be to spot financial products that hurt ordinary consumers, such as loans or fees that trap people in debt, and to ban or restrict them. It would have given the agency power to write safety rules for lenders, run a consumer complaint hotline, study industry practices, levy fines, and let consumers and states sue over violations. The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Financial Services Committee until Congress ended. A version of the idea later became law in a different form: the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, created by the 2010 Dodd-Frank law.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers — including small businesses, which the bill counts as "consumers" — would have gained a regulator focused on whether credit cards, loans, and deposit products are designed to be understood and repaid, plus a hotline, fines against abusive lenders, and new private rights to sue with minimum damages of $1,000 per violation plus attorney fees [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Creates a five-member commission with a single mission: to identify and ban consumer financial products and practices that are abusive, fraudulent, unfair, deceptive, or predatory, modeled loosely on how the Consumer Product Safety Commission recalls dangerous toys.
Gives consumers a complaint hotline, public reports on industry problems, and the right to sue lenders directly, with statutory damages of at least $1,000 per violation plus attorney fees.
Requires lenders to assess a borrower's ability to repay before extending credit, and allows state regulators and courts to enforce even stronger consumer protections than the federal rules.

analysis.who_pays: Banks, credit card issuers, and consumer lenders would bear compliance costs, fines, and the loss of products the commission banned; the commission itself would be funded by appropriations [S3]. Some of these costs could be passed to borrowers as higher prices or tighter credit.

drawbacks.text: The bill's language is broad — it bans any practice that is 'abusive, fraudulent, unfair, deceptive, predatory, anticompetitive, or otherwise anticonsumer' — leaving the new commission wide discretion to decide what products are unsafe, which critics warned could restrict access to legitimate credit.

It would have created another overlapping federal regulator on top of the nine existing banking and consumer agencies, raising compliance costs for lenders large and small — costs that could be passed on to borrowers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — a single regulator whose job was to stop predatory financial products before they spread, plus a complaint hotline and private lawsuits for consumers — was large, and the main cost was compliance and uncertainty for banks and lenders whose profits came from fees and risky products. The bill was broad in wording, so regulators would have had wide discretion about what counts as "unreasonable" risk, which is a real objection. On balance it would have shifted bargaining power toward consumers, and its core idea was adopted later in diluted form as the CFPB.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, which never acted on it, so it sat and expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 25, 2009, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services.
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

The bill's findings blamed a fragmented regulatory structure for letting 'excessively costly or predatory' financial products flourish, and proposed a single agency whose sole job was consumer financial product safety.

The idea did not fully disappear: its core concept — a dedicated consumer financial regulator with rulemaking, hotline, and state-enforcement powers — reappeared in altered form in the Dodd-Frank financial reform law of 2010 as the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lenders and financial firms that profit from fees and hard-to-understand products kept operating under the fragmented regulatory system the bill criticized, with no dedicated consumer-safety regulator created by this bill.

for.name: Rep. Bill Delahunt
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 25, 2009, with Rep. Miller of North Carolina.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, letting it die in committee without a vote.

against.name: Banking and financial services industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed creating a standalone consumer financial regulator during the 2009-2010 financial reform debate, favoring oversight spread across existing banking agencies.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 cosponsors were Democrats in a Democratic-controlled House, and the bill received no Republican support; it also never advanced, so there was no vote to measure.

industries.note: The bill would have allowed a dedicated regulator to ban fees, products, and collection practices that these firms profit from, such as lending without verifying ability to repay. Its finding section says the absence of oversight allowed predatory products to flourish.

industries.industry: Mortgage lenders and credit card issuers
industries.note: They faced the same new policing and penalties per transaction, but the bill also promised 'regulatory certainty' by consolidating consumer rules and superseding weaker agency rules with stronger ones. Its defeat preserved the fragmented, industry-friendlier status quo.
